sql_threads.py:37-46 uses a module-level ThreadPoolExecutor with loop.run_in_executor. In CPython, run_in_executor wraps the concurrent future with wrap_future, and cancelling the asyncio future calls concurrent Future.cancel(). A still-queued item is cancelled, and the worker's set_running_or_notify_cancel() returns False, so the call is skipped and never started. concurrent.futures.thread registers _python_exit through threading._register_atexit. That hook joins all executor threads at exit, so no user shutdown hook is needed. Started work is not interrupted, and exit waits for it. This matches the claim and the module docstring at lines 16-20. This rests on my knowledge of CPython; I did not read the CPython source in this environment.

sql_threads.py:37-46 creates a private ThreadPoolExecutor and run_blocking_sql passes it explicitly to loop.run_in_executor, so it never touches the default executor. Grep of src/ shows _EXECUTOR is referenced only in that file. asyncio.to_thread appears only at profiles.py:219 (profile-store write, default executor). The chromadb agent_memory run_in_executor calls use self._executor, which does not import sql_threads. No set_default_executor call exists. No path routes default-executor work through the SQL pool, or SQL work through the default executor.

sql_threads.py:45-46 uses functools.partial(contextvars.copy_context().run, func, *args) with loop.run_in_executor, which is the same mechanism as CPython asyncio.to_thread (copy_context().run via partial into run_in_executor). The context is copied on the event-loop thread at call time. runtime.py has a single ContextVar, _PROFILE_VAR (line 54) holding EffectiveSettings, read via .get() at line 82. A copied context carries it, so the row cap and every other EffectiveSettings field are visible in the worker. The trace input was a ContextVar set after the call; it is not copied, and the docstring does not claim it would be.

Postgres: postgres/sql_runner.py:147-153 issues session-level SET statement_timeout before both read (named cursor) and write paths, so it applies to every statement. MySQL: mysql/sql_runner.py:115-122 sets SESSION MAX_EXECUTION_TIME, which MySQL limits to SELECT (comment at :116), so a write with read_only=false is unbounded. SQLite: sqlite/sql_runner.py:99 connects with default timeout (Python sqlite3 default 5s busy timeout), the progress handler is registered only at :121-125 after connect, and covers cursor.execute/fetchmany (:127-131); it is not invoked during busy-wait, so lock waits are bounded by the busy timeout. Falsifying input (long MySQL write, lock-blocked SQLite connect) behaves as the doc states.

Fixed at head. sql_threads.py:34-39 defines a dedicated ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=SQL_WORKER_THREADS=8), and run_blocking_sql (42-46) uses loop.run_in_executor(_EXECUTOR,...). All three runners call run_blocking_sql (postgres sql_runner.py:124, mysql:91, sqlite:92), so none use asyncio.to_thread. The only remaining asyncio.to_thread is profiles.py:219 (atomic_write_text), on the default executor, so profile writes no longer queue behind SQL. Concurrency is bounded at 8; queued calls drop on cancel. A started query cannot be interrupted, and statement_timeout_ms=0 still disables its bound. The module docstring (16-20) documents both, and the finding's remedy was the dedicated sized executor.

The unqualified sentence no longer appears at head. sql_threads.py:16-20 now says the thread stays in use until the driver returns and that statement_timeout_ms ends it early only for the statements each runner applies it to, and that 0 disables it. transport.md:116 spells out the limits: 0 disables the timeout everywhere, Postgres applies SET statement_timeout to every statement, MySQL MAX_EXECUTION_TIME covers only SELECT (a write with read_only=false is not bounded), and SQLite's progress handler does not cover connect or lock wait (the default busy timeout bounds those instead). A grep of the three sql_runner.py files for 'driver returns', 'still runs', 'cannot be interrupted' and 'timeout bounds' found no leftover claim. The runners' timeout code is consistent with the docs: postgres:147-152, mysql:108-122, sqlite:121-139. I did not re-read the full MySQL and SQLite run_sql bodies.
